title: Vitamin D Deficiency and Strength Training: Why Fall and Winter Workouts Feel Heavier
description: As sunlight fades, low vitamin D can mean heavier-feeling sessions, lingering soreness, and higher stress-fracture risk for women who lift. What the research shows, who should test, and how to fix low levels safely.
author: Sundee Fundee Team

bestFor: Women who lift and train indoors through fall and winter — especially anyone whose sessions feel heavier, whose soreness lingers, or who has a stress-fracture history — and want to know whether low vitamin D is worth testing for, what the evidence says about strength and recovery, and how to correct low levels without megadosing.
body:
Every fall, somewhere around the time the morning workout moves back indoors, a familiar complaint shows up: sessions that felt fine in August suddenly feel heavy, soreness lingers, and the whole thing gets blamed on darkness and desk weather. Some of that is scheduling and mood. But there's a real physiological variable changing too — vitamin D — and for women who lift, it's worth understanding what it can and can't do to your training before you either ignore it or megadose it.

Here's the honest headline from the research: correcting a genuine vitamin D deficiency is worth doing and may matter for muscle function, recovery, and injury risk. Taking large doses on top of adequate levels, on the other hand, has repeatedly failed to improve performance in trials. The skill is figuring out which category you're in — and that's exactly what this article walks through.

## What Vitamin D Actually Does in a Training Body

Vitamin D is best known for its role in bone: it governs how well you absorb calcium, which is why deficiency in children causes rickets and in adults can contribute to soft, achy bones. But muscle tissue has vitamin D receptors too, and the nutrient is involved in muscle fiber function and repair. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements lists muscle weakness, fatigue, and bone or muscle aches among the symptoms associated with deficiency — not the dramatic weakness of severe disease, but the low-grade version that reads, from inside a training block, as "everything feels harder than it should."

For lifters, two implications matter most. First, chronic low-grade fatigue and nagging heaviness in fall and winter may have a nutrient component, not just a scheduling one. Second — and this connects directly to bone — vitamin D status is part of the load-bearing foundation that lets you train hard for decades — the same foundation our guide to [strength training for bone density](/blog/strength-training-for-bone-density) covers from the loading side — which is why it sits alongside protein and progressive overload in the long-game categories rather than the quick-fix ones.

## Why Lifters Run Low as the Days Shorten

Your skin makes vitamin D from UVB sunlight, and the supply chain breaks down quickly in autumn: the sun sits lower, UVB intensity drops at most latitudes, sessions move indoors, and skin stays covered. Add sunscreen (correctly worn for skin health) and shorter outdoor windows, and cutaneous production falls off a cliff. Body fat also stores vitamin D and can sequester it, and darker skin synthesizes less from the same sun exposure — both are risk factors the NIH fact sheet calls out.

How common is this even in athletes? Higher than you'd guess. In one randomized trial published in 2026, professional female soccer players tested in the autumn — right after a summer of outdoor training — still had 1 in 4 sitting at insufficient or deficient levels. Reviews of female athletes consistently flag suboptimal status, especially in athletes who train primarily indoors. If professional athletes with outdoor jobs run low by September, a lifter training in a windowless gym has no reason for complacency.

## What the Evidence Says About Strength and Recovery

This is where honesty matters, because the supplement industry has outrun the data.

The deficiency side is reasonably solid: low vitamin D status is consistently associated with musculoskeletal symptoms, and a 2025 review of studies in injured individuals and athletes found supplementation reduced stress-fracture incidence, even while results on muscle function itself were mixed. Bone stress injuries are exactly the injury you don't want as a lifter, so the injury signal alone justifies caring about status.

The performance side is weaker. The soccer RCT above supplemented at 4,000 IU per day for eight weeks — a meaningful dose — and found blood levels rose nicely while performance measures didn't move. A 2026 review of supplementation and physical performance reached the same conclusion from broader data: benefits concentrate in older, clinical, or deficient populations, while effects in athletes with adequate levels are inconsistent and often null.

Translated for the platform: if you're deficient, fixing it may remove a real drag on training and lower injury risk. If you're replete, more vitamin D is not a performance supplement — there is no evidence it adds strength on top of adequate, and megadosing carries real risks, including dangerously high calcium over time.

## Should You Get Tested?

The relevant blood test is 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Levels below 20 ng/mL are generally considered inadequate for bone health by the NIH. Routine screening of every healthy adult isn't universally recommended — but a targeted test makes sense when symptoms and risk factors stack up: persistent fatigue or heavier-feeling sessions through the dark months, training mostly indoors, living at a northern latitude, darker skin, higher body fat, or a history of stress injuries. If that list describes you, it's a reasonable thing to raise at your next appointment or annual bloodwork rather than guessing.

Timing matters less than people think — although levels naturally peak in late summer and bottom out at the end of winter, a low-normal reading in October is more informative than a reassuring one taken in August.

## Fixing Low Vitamin D Safely

If levels come back low, the fix is usually unglamorous and effective:

- **Supplement moderately.** The NIH recommended intake is 600 IU daily for adults up to 70 (800 after that), and the tolerable upper limit for self-supplementing is 4,000 IU per day. Deficiency treatment sometimes uses short, higher-dose protocols — that's prescriber territory, not DIY.
- **Eat the sources that exist.** Fatty fish like salmon, fortified milk and yogurt, eggs, and UV-treated mushrooms carry meaningful amounts, though food alone rarely corrects a true deficiency.
- **Use what sun remains.** A midday walk still helps in early fall; by late November at most latitudes north of roughly Atlanta or Los Angeles, UVB is too weak for meaningful synthesis until spring.
- **Don't megadose.** Vitamin D is fat-soluble and accumulates. Toxicity is rare but real, and it arrives through exactly the kind of "if 2,000 IU works, 10,000 works better" logic that this article exists to deflate.

One practical note for lifters specifically: take it with a meal containing fat — absorption is better, and pairing it with breakfast anchors the habit.

## When Fatigue Isn't Vitamin D

Low vitamin D produces a fatigue that mimics several other common ones, and more than one can be true at once. Before crediting or clearing vitamin D, run the standard stack: iron status ([low ferritin](/blog/low-ferritin-strength-training-women) and low vitamin D travel together in heavily menstruating lifters), thyroid function (constant, non-cyclical exhaustion is the pattern our [hypothyroidism guide](/blog/strength-training-with-hypothyroidism-women) explains — and it deserves labs), and [sleep debt](/blog/strength-training-after-bad-sleep), which remains the most common cause by volume. If your energy instead tracks a monthly pattern, that points to [cycle-related fatigue](/blog/period-fatigue-strength-training) rather than a micronutrient. Sorting this out is exactly why a targeted blood panel beats self-diagnosis by symptom checklist.

## What to Do Next

- **Symptoms plus risk factors (indoor training, northern latitude, dark months):** raise 25(OH)D testing at your next checkup; meanwhile, a daily 600–1,000 IU supplement with breakfast is a low-risk holding pattern.
- **Tested and low:** follow your clinician's correction protocol, recheck after repletion, and treat bone health as part of your programming, not a footnote.
- **Tested and adequate:** you're done — no performance bonus exists above adequate, so save the money for protein.
- **Undecided:** the cheap, reversible move is moderate-dose supplementation through winter plus a reevaluation in spring.

## The Bottom Line

Vitamin D is not a strength supplement, and the trials are refreshingly blunt about that. It's a floor: keeping your levels above deficiency removes a known drag on bone, muscle function, and recovery, and lowers stress-fracture risk. As the light fades for the season, the move isn't megadosing on hope — it's testing if your symptoms and situation warrant it, correcting a true deficiency at sensible doses, and letting the barbell do the rest.
